analysis.one_liner: Bars rental companies from renting or selling vehicles under open federal safety recalls.
analysis.headline: Introduced in September 2014 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, the bill never received a hearing or a vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law since 2000 has barred new-car dealers from selling or leasing a vehicle before an open safety recall is fixed, but rental companies were not covered, so a renter could be handed a car the manufacturer had recalled. This bill would have applied the same rule to rental companies: after getting the manufacturer's recall notice, they would have had to stop renting (and selling) affected vehicles within 24 hours, or 48 hours for recalls covering more than 5,000 vehicles in their fleet. It also let regulators inspect rental companies' records during safety investigations and required a study of recall completion on rental trucks.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of Americans who rent cars each year. They could no longer be handed a vehicle with an unfixed safety defect the manufacturer had already recalled, such as a faulty steering part or brake component.

how_it_helps.text: A rental company could rent, sell, or lease a covered vehicle only after the recall defect or federal safety-standard violation is remedied [S2].
Compliance would be required within 24 hours of receiving the manufacturer's notice, extended to 48 hours when a recall covers more than 5,000 vehicles in the company's fleet [S2][S3].
The same recall prohibition already applied to new-car dealers under existing law; the bill extended that rule to rental companies [S3].
Regulators could inspect rental companies' records during safety investigations and require compliance recordkeeping, and a study of recall completion on rental trucks would be mandatory [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Rental car companies, which would bear the cost of pulling recalled vehicles from their fleets on short notice, keeping them idle until fixed, and tracking notices across large fleets — costs that could flow into rental prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill shields vehicle manufacturers: nothing in it creates or increases any manufacturer's liability for a recalled vehicle, and it leaves manufacturer-rental company contracts untouched, so makers of defective vehicles would bear no new responsibility [S2][S3].

Complying within 24 hours with a fleet-wide recall notice is operationally demanding for rental companies, and the bill allows renting (though not selling) a recalled vehicle if the notice spells out temporary fixes that eliminate the safety risk — a reliance on the manufacturer's judgment about what makes a recalled car safe to drive [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is direct and serious: renters would stop being handed cars with known, unfixed safety defects, closing a gap that has applied to dealers since 2000. The main costs fall on rental companies as fleet downtime and logistics, which are real but limited, and the 48-hour window for very large recalls acknowledges that. The notable weakness is a liability shield for the manufacturers whose defects cause the recalls, leaving the deepest pocket partly off the hook.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator Charles Schumer introduced the bill with seven Democratic cosponsors on September 16, 2014 [S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote after the referral; the bill never advanced before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Rental car companies came out ahead: they kept the freedom to rent and sell vehicles under open safety recalls and avoided the 24- to 48-hour compliance costs, while renters gained no new protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rental car companies kept the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and because the bill never reached a vote there is no record of how anyone else would have voted [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would have required them to pull recalled vehicles off rental lots within 24 hours (48 for recalls over 5,000 vehicles) and keep them out of service until fixed, creating fleet downtime and compliance costs. Their interest in avoiding those costs runs directly against renters' interest in not driving recalled cars [S2][S3].

Their existing duty to issue recall notices was unchanged, and the bill added a provision that no new liability could be created or increased for a manufacturer of a recalled vehicle. The shield protects makers of defective vehicles at some cost to injured consumers [S2][S3].
